doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: Song titles and 'Waiting for Chet'
summary: Titles come from personal experience or poetic ideas; he explains he sets up tunes by playing on the changes and no longer announces them.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Does that concept, this is a bit of a tangent but — apply to when it comes to put a title on one of your compositions? Where do your song titles come from?
Usually a personal experience. Sometimes a personal experience. Sometimes it’s just looking for a good poetic title you know.
Yeah I was listening to you play I think it’s “Waiting for Chet.” “Waiting for Chet.”
And I was trying to tell if the beginning, you were playing by yourself I think. If the bass player was there I couldn’t hear it ‘cause of the recording, but —

It was just focused on you and you had all these flurry of chords going by and I couldn’t tell if you were setting up the group or if this was the actual composition. I’m not really expecting you to —

Yeah I was setting it up. I don’t play the head until after my exposition you know, in front. I’m playing on the changes and stuff you know, and the guys recognize it. I don’t even have to tell them what I’m doing. As a matter of fact I don’t even announce the tunes to them anymore, I just start playing. Because I don’t know what I’m going to do next you know.
